lessons.title: The milking routine
lessons.html:
Why routine matters

Milk let-down is controlled by the hormone oxytocin, released when the cow is calm and her teats are stimulated. Stress releases adrenaline, which blocks let-down. A calm, consistent routine at the same times every day gives faster milking, more complete milk-out, healthier udders and cleaner milk.

Before milking

  • Check the plant: clean, assembled correctly, vacuum at the right level, pulsators working.
  • Check the bulk tank is clean, empty and the cooling system ready.
  • Milkers wear clean clothing and gloves; gloves reduce the spread of mastitis bacteria between cows.
  • Bring cows in quietly; no dogs, shouting or sticks.

Milking steps

  1. Forestrip a few squirts from each teat into a strip cup and check for clots, flakes or watery milk, which indicate clinical mastitis.
  2. Pre-dip or clean teats as the farm protocol says, and wipe each cow's teats dry with a separate paper towel or cloth.
  3. Attach the cluster within the time set by the farm after stimulation, so it coincides with let-down; avoid air entering the liners.
  4. Adjust the cluster so it hangs straight and does not slip.
  5. Remove when milk flow drops, by cutting vacuum first. Automatic cluster removers do this; avoid overmilking, which damages teat ends.
  6. Post-dip every teat fully with teat dip immediately after removal.

Special cows

  • Cows with clinical mastitis or under treatment are marked and milked last or with a separate unit, and their milk is kept out of the bulk tank.
  • Fresh cows produce colostrum, which is not sold as milk; keep it separate for calves.

Safety

Stand where cows cannot kick you, use rubber mats and good footwear on wet floors, and keep hands clear of moving gates and rotary platforms.

lessons.title: Milk cooling, plant cleaning and quality
lessons.html:
Cooling the milk

Milk leaves the cow at body temperature, ideal for bacteria. Fast cooling is the main defence against high bacterial counts.

  • Many farms use a plate cooler with cold water to pre-cool milk before it reaches the bulk tank.
  • The bulk tank must cool milk to the required storage temperature within the required time; follow the hygiene regulations and buyer standards that apply to your farm.
  • Check and record tank temperature at set times; act immediately on cooling failures.
  • Keep the agitator running as designed so milk cools evenly.
  • Have a generator or backup plan for power failures.

Cleaning the milking plant and tank

Milk residues left in the plant feed bacteria. A standard cleaning cycle is:

  1. Rinse with lukewarm water to remove milk residues.
  2. Hot detergent wash with an alkaline detergent at the temperature and concentration on the product label.
  3. Acid rinse as scheduled, to remove milkstone and minerals.
  4. Sanitise before the next milking where required.

Check wash water temperature, detergent dosing and that every part is reached. Replace rubber liners and tubes at the intervals the manufacturer recommends; worn liners harbour bacteria and milk poorly. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling detergents and acids, never mix chemicals, and store them away from the milk room.

Milk quality tests

TestWhat it tells you
Somatic cell count (SCC)Udder health
Bacterial countHygiene of milking, cleaning and cooling
Antibiotic residue testTreated milk entering the tank
Butterfat and proteinComposition for payment and feeding
Added water (freezing point)Dilution

The California Mastitis Test (CMT) can be used at cow side to find quarters with high cell counts.

In-parlour records

Record milking times, tank temperatures, cleaning checks, treated cows and milk dumped. These records support quality claims and help trace problems.

Key points

  • A calm, consistent routine supports let-down and udder health.
  • Forestrip, clean and dry, attach at let-down, avoid overmilking, post-dip every teat.
  • Keep treated cows' milk and colostrum out of the bulk tank.
  • Cool milk quickly and record tank temperatures.
  • Clean the plant with rinse, hot alkaline wash, acid rinse and sanitising as scheduled.
